header: Date: 2027-06-15 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM); Sara Lopez (Nimbus Head of ML), Michael King (Infra), Rohit Patel (CTO), Emma Zhao (SRE)
summary: POC scoping focused on benchmark planning and harness integration. Discussed success criteria (latency, throughput, cost), workload sizing (QPS, concurrency, token lengths), streaming vs non-streaming test plans, security prerequisites, and timelines for initial runs. Agreed next steps: share benchmark template, customer to provide scripts and sample data, schedule initial non-streaming run, follow-up to plan streaming runs and Dedicated capacity options.
topics: Workload sizing: QPS, concurrency, token lengths
Benchmark harness integration and customer scripts
Security and network prerequisites (VPC, KMS, SOC2)
Timeline and next steps for POC runs
transcript: [00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh quick intro, i'm Alex from Redwood AE, with Priya SE and Jordan on CSM. uh Sara, do you want to quickly intro the goals from Nimbus?

[00:12] Sara Lopez: Sure, thanks. Hi all. Our main goal is to validate cost and latency for two primary workloads: conversational customer support (streaming) and nightly batch summarization (non-streaming). Success metric is 95th perc latency < 300ms for support, and cost per 1k tokens under our target. We'll also need production-like traffic—roughly 150 qps peak for support and concurrent batch jobs of 20 runners.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Got it. That helps. quick clarifying q: when you say 150 qps is that per region or global?
[00:42] Michael King: That's per region, primarily us-east and eu-west. We expect failover to secondary region but initial run is us-east.

[00:50] Alex Chen: Ok, cool. For the POC we usually align on three things: success criteria, workload specs and harness integration. We'll send a benchmark template, but today we want to map your scripts to our harness and decide streaming vs non-streaming ordering.
[01:05] Rohit Patel: One thing from infra: we prefer private deployment or a Dedicated pool due to data residency. we need to know what data persists in logs and whether KMS is used.

[01:14] Priya Nair: Short answer — we can run Dedicated or Private. logs and audit go to customer-controlled S3 for Private and you can integrate KMS. We'll include SOC2 compliance docs. we'll follow up with the security pack. (note: transcript sometimes shows KMS as "K-M-S")

[01:30] Sara Lopez: Great. on the scripts, we have two folders: support_streaming/ with websocket-based client that sends small incremental tokens, and batch_summarize/ which posts full documents. We'll share 10 sample sessions and 500 sample docs.

[01:45] Alex Chen: Perfect. For the harness we support both a streaming runner and a non-streaming runner. streaming tests are more sensitive to tail latency and socket handling; non-streaming tests are easier for throughput numbers. Ideally we run non-streaming first to get baseline throughput/cost, then streaming for tail latency.

[02:05] Michael King: question: does your harness replay websocket frames exactly as our client does? we have partial chunks that are smaller than typical examples. sometimes the kv cash and cache warmups matter.

[02:16] Priya Nair: We can replay websocket frames; SE tooling supports chunked frames and can model your inter-arrival timing. we do occasionally transcribe "KV cache" as "KV cash" in docs, but functionality works. we'll need your client stub or a recorded trace so we can emulate accurately.

[02:33] Sara Lopez: we'll share a recorded trace and a simple node/python client. also note our support model uses function calling for retrieval, so the harness should capture function call overheads.
[02:45] Alex Chen: Good note — include function call latency in the script. For sizing: can you confirm average and 95th token lengths for support?

[02:52] Sara Lopez: Avg 120 tokens per turn, 95th is about 700 tokens during long context. batch docs average 4k tokens compressed, but we'll send raw. concurrency for batch is roughly 20 parallel workers.

[03:04] Priya Nair: That's helpful. For throughput planning we'll parameterize: concurrency, qps per connection, average token length, and average model. Which model family do you want to test? open to Redwood-verified Llama variants or one of your licensed models?

[03:18] Rohit Patel: We prefer an open model that's similar to Llama 3 size-wise, quantized, since we want to avoid external provider vendor lock-in. but we need to compare to Anthropic-ish baselines for cost/latency.
[03:28] Alex Chen: Ok we'll propose a baseline model and a lower-cost quantized variant for throughput. SE will recommend kernel/quantization profiles. Priya, add model mapping note.

[03:36] Priya Nair: noted. For the bench harness steps, recommended order: 1) ingest sample dataset, 2) run non-streaming throughput sweep (vary concurrency to find optimal batching), 3) run streaming tail-latency tests under simulated arrival patterns, 4) run fallback and capacity stress with model variants. We'll instrument token-level latency and per-route cost.
[03:56] Emma Zhao: For networking, we'll provide a VPC peering diagram. we need to confirm outbound egress to your benchmarking endpoint if hosted; if Dedicated we prefer no egress.

[04:07] Alex Chen: Noted. We'll prepare both hosted and Dedicated runbooks. For hosted we'll require IP allowlist and short-term credentials; for Dedicated/Private we'll run inside customer VPC with no egress and deliver logs to your S3.
[04:18] Michael King: On metrics, we need to see 95/99 latency, p50, cost per 1k tokens, and GPU utilization. Also tokenization differences — token counts must be consistent across runs.
[04:28] Priya Nair: We'll include a tokenizer sanity check in the harness and produce token-diff reports. sometimes model tokenizer variations cause 5-8% delta — we'll call that out in the report.
[04:40] Sara Lopez: timeline question: how long to get an initial set of bench numbers?

[04:45] Alex Chen: If we receive scripts + sample data by 6/20, we can run the initial non-streaming sweep the week of 6/21 and deliver a preliminary report by 6/25. Streaming tails will take an extra run and analysis, estimate the follow-up by 7/2.
[04:58] Rohit Patel: Will you need Dedicated GPUs for the streaming runs?

[05:02] Priya Nair: For production-like tail latency it's helpful to run on Dedicated GPU pools to mirror real capacity. For evaluation we can simulate on hosted but it's less accurate for true 95/99 tails. We'll flag the differences in the notes.

[05:15] Sara Lopez: Ok makes sense. Regarding success criteria, our internal bar: 95th < 300ms for streaming, 99th < 500ms ideally, throughput to handle 150 qps with <2% error. Cost target is $X per 1k tokens — we'll include exact number in scripts.
[05:35] Alex Chen: Excellent. We'll add those thresholds to the template. Any compliance blockers?
[05:39] Emma Zhao: We need SOC2 attestations, SSO/SAML integration detail for RBAC, and confirmation on customer-managed KMS in Private mode. Also audit log retention for 13 months.

[05:51] Priya Nair: We can provide SOC2 and SAML docs; audit logs configurable retention — we'll share options. KMS integration supported for Private deployments. we'll attach security pack in the follow-up email.
[06:05] Michael King: small note — some of our batch jobs use long context recompute with KV cache reuse, can the harness simulate cache warm starts?

[06:13] Priya Nair: Yes, harness supports KV cache warmups and prefix caching; we might call it "prefix warmup" in notes. sometimes transcripts spell it KV "cash" but functionality included. we'll include cache-warm up waveform in the script.
[06:26] Alex Chen: Great. Let's capture concrete deliverables and owners now so we don't lose them. Jordan, can you read back?

[06:32] Jordan Lee: Sure. Action items: Alex will send benchmark template and proposed models/pricing by 6/18; Sara will share scripts + sample data by 6/20; Priya will prepare streaming runbook and quantization recommendations by 6/20; Emma to provide VPC/network diagram by 6/19. We'll schedule initial non-streaming run the week of 6/21. Does that match folks?
[06:52] Sara Lopez: yes matches. quick clarification — in the harness, will you run exactly our Node websocket client or a replay?
[06:59] Priya Nair: We'll run both options: replay of traces for parity and a live-run with your client if you can provide a small stub. live-run helps uncover socket-level differences.
[07:09] Rohit Patel: On the commercial side, what's trial cost if we need Dedicated?

[07:13] Alex Chen: For POCs we offer a limited Dedicated credit; i'll include Dedicated pricing bands in the follow-up. The template will also include the expected hardware sizes so you can estimate costs.
[07:24] Michael King: Any quirks about streaming vs non-streaming in terms of batching?

[07:28] Priya Nair: Streaming avoids large micro-batching across requests because of per-connection realtime needs; instead we optimize kernel selection and low-latency execution paths. Non-streaming benefits more from continuous batching and larger token batch sizes. We will show both profiles in the report.
[07:45] Sara Lopez: Great. Also include an analysis of model quantization impact on quality — we don't want regressions above 2% on rouge/accuracy for summarization.

[07:54] Priya Nair: We'll run quality checks and include regression deltas tied to specific prompt sets. we'll also tie quality regression alerts into the Optimize recommendations so you can see cost/quality tradeoffs.
[08:06] Alex Chen: Any other risks we should call out?
[08:09] Emma Zhao: Network egress and peering approvals are sometimes slow — please note that we'll need firewall rules and a security contact to expedite.

[08:16] Alex Chen: Noted — we'll include an expedite checklist. Ok final recap: we'll send the template and security pack, customer shares scripts and network diagram, we run non-streaming baseline the week of 6/21, then streaming follow-up. next meeting to review results tentatively 6/28. Thanks everyone.
[08:33] Sara Lopez: Thanks all, bye.
[08:36] Alex Chen: Bye.
[62:00] <meeting ended>
